newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Ebola has killed 43 in Gabon since July, WHO says.
newsitem.headline: Ebola has killed 43 in Gabon since July, WHO says.

text.p: Forty-three people have died from Ebola haemorrhagic fever in Gabon since July, where a prolonged outbreak has struck 58 victims, the World Health Organisation (WHO) said on Friday.

But the United Nations health agency said that Gabon's Ministry of Health had taken every precaution to stem the lethal virus from spreading, and WHO did not recommend restricting travel to and from the West African country.

Most cases and deaths occurred in the area of Booue, some 470 kms (nearly 300 miles) east of Libreville, according to a WHO statement. The nationwide toll includes nine cases, eight of them fatal, in the capital.
"Since July 1996, there have been 58 cases including the 43 deaths, one hospitalised case in Booue and 14 people who have been discharged from hospital after recovery," it said.
"There are currently no known cases in Libreville."

All recent cases in Libreville belong to the same household and occurred following close contact with Libreville inhabitants at the burial of a relative who died in late November from Ebola in a village near Booue, according to the statement.
The most recent Ebola patient died in hospital on Wednesday, and people he had contact with are being followed closely.
In all, 167 people in Booue and Libreville who have had possible physical contact with Ebola patients remain under daily surveillance, according to the Geneva-based agency.
The outbreak began last July with the death of a hunter in a logging camp near Booue, in Oogue-Ivindo province. The next case was a friend, followed by a traditional healer and his aide.

There is no specific treatment or vaccine for Ebola, one of the most virulent viral diseases known, which kills between 50 and 90 percent of its victims. It is spead by direct contact with body fluids such as blood, vomit, and diarrhoea.
Patients suffer fever, diarrhoea, vomiting and eventually haemorrhaging and signs of kidney and liver failure. The incubation period is between two and 21 days.
Some 245 people died in 1995 in an epidemic around Kikwit, Zaire, the country where the virus was first identified in 1976.
A single victim in Ivory Coast in December 1995 survived.
